chapters.title: The Secret of Happiness
chapters.hook: A thank-you email leaves drafts, and a treadmill belt keeps moving before the win arrives.
chapters.counterintuition: Despite the usual success-then-happiness story, the happiness lesson puts practice first. The small rep comes before the proof, so your next action has better ground under it.
chapters.tryThisNow: Within the next 24 hours, the first time you open your laptop lid, write 3 new things you are grateful for and put a check beside each.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Happiness works on the slight edge when you practice it first: mark 3 new things, send thanks, move your body, and let that better state support the next choice.

breakdown.fastRead: The renewal notice slides into an inbox while the person behind it waits to feel better after the next win. That delay has a cost: the old subscription renews, the missed call stays missed, and the day begins with a quiet leak. The happiness claim flips the order. Shawn Achor's The Happiness Advantage gives the frame: happiness before success. Joy practiced early changes the work that follows. Mark one small rep, such as 3 new things that make you grateful or a short cardio rep, before the mood gets a vote. A checked box beats a wished-for mood.
breakdown.deepRead:
Yann reaches for his launch notes with a tight jaw, and the next task looks heavier than it is. That is why the order matters. The review of Shawn Achor says happiness can support brains and bodies, productivity, confidence, positivity, bravery, consciousness, and motivation. You do not need to stretch that into magic. You only need the plain edge: a better state can make the next useful act easier to start and easier to repeat.

A blank line in a notebook keeps the claim honest. No one has to become bright by force. The list gives small handles. Write 3 new things you are grateful for, spend 2 minutes on a positive past experience, sit for a few minutes, send praise or thanks, or do 15 minutes of cardio. Those handles move happiness from weather to behavior. When the behavior is visible, you can repeat it.

Rachel sees this during onboarding. A new hire says gratitude is too soft for a busy week. Rachel writes 3 new things on the board and asks for fresh entries, not the same safe answer. The room changes because confusion becomes material. The learner can see the difference between "be more positive" and "write the next grateful item."

Your pen makes the move visible. Make a small box beside the practice, do the rep, and check it. The mark is not decoration. It shows that happiness was practiced before success had a chance to approve it. Happiness is fuel, not a finish line.
breakdown.fullRead:
Nancy's pen is already crossing cardio off the training plan when Rachel writes it back in. They are equals, so no title can settle the dispute. Nancy sees a crowded day and wants every spare minute for results. Rachel sees the same day and asks why the state that helps results should be saved for later. One of them has to yield, but the yield is not defeat. It is a better read of the order.

That order is the clean edge of the anniversary material. Happiness is not treated as decoration for a finished life. It is practiced while the life is still messy. Shawn Achor's The Happiness Advantage gives the outside frame, and the review makes the claim practical: a happier outlook can help the next hard action start with more nerve and drive. The practice does not ask you to pretend every day feels good. It asks you to stop making a good feeling wait outside the door.

The source list is a menu: gratitude, positive journaling, meditation, praise, cardio, savoring, forgiveness, giving, and reading. Some are private. Some involve another person. Some use the body. Some use a page. That spread matters because a single habit can become another excuse. If you miss the morning note, you can still send thanks. If your head is full, you can take the short cardio slot. If your body is spent, you can read 10 pages or savor one good thing without turning it into a project.

Janet's planning choice shows the practical side. She has a porch step, a warm phone, and a day that has already spent most of her attention. A giant happiness plan would fail before it started. A single checked rep can survive. She can budget the next day by placing one small practice where her hand already goes: the laptop lid, the kettle, the door handle. The cue matters because the old order is strong. Without a cue, success keeps making promises happiness has to wait for.

This is also where the idea can go bad. Happiness practice can become another way to scold yourself. It can turn into a bright mask over grief, a forced smile at work, or a rule that makes tired people feel guilty for being tired. That is not the slight edge. The rep should support the truth, not hide it. Gratitude can sit beside pain. Cardio can help a hard day without denying that the day was hard. Praise can be real thanks, not a bribe for approval.

The practice curdles when it becomes a mask. If you use gratitude to dodge grief, cardio to outrun every hard talk, or praise to buy approval, the slight edge has become another way to fake being fine. Let the rep support the truth. Do not make it hide the truth.

examples.title: Locker Room Reframe
examples.scenario: "Stop making happiness the bonus prize," the coach says in the gym locker room as Yann folds his work shirt over a bench. Yann has been reading Shawn Achor's The Happiness Advantage, but happiness before success still sounds backwards with launch day near. The coach points to the order: practice the state that helps the work, then ship.
examples.whatToDo: Yann marks one small happiness rep before he checks launch messages. He lets Shawn Achor's order guide the morning instead of waiting for success to grant relief.
examples.whyItMatters: The reframe makes happiness before success usable. A reader can practice the state that supports the work before the work has paid out.

examples.title: Board Of New Things
examples.scenario: The dry-erase marker squeaks across the onboarding board while Rachel waits for the new hires to name any useful habit. A student says gratitude is just a warmer mood. Rachel writes "3 new things" and asks the class to make each one new and grateful, not recycled. The confusion becomes the lesson: a daily exercise needs a count.
examples.whatToDo: Rachel turns the class away from a vague mood word. She asks for 3 new things, checks that each item is grateful and fresh, then lets the count carry the practice.
examples.whyItMatters: A count makes the gratitude practice testable. The reader can tell whether the daily exercise happened, instead of hoping a general attitude changed.

examples.title: Family Call Warm-Up
examples.scenario: Her sister's tablet dies, and Hailey gets handed the family video call warm-up with everyone already restless. Last week she opened by asking for good news and watched silence spread. Now she asks for 3 new things each person is grateful for, one at a time. The call is not perfect, but the first answers are easier to hear.
examples.whatToDo: Hailey changes only the opener. She replaces a broad mood request with 3 new things, then waits for each grateful answer to land before moving on.
examples.whyItMatters: The contrast carries the lesson. A small daily exercise can work in ordinary family life because it gives people a concrete first step.

examples.title: Cardio Stays In
examples.scenario: Nancy is crossing 15 minutes of cardio off the staff training plan at the reception desk while Rachel writes it back in. "We need that slot for the success metrics," Nancy says. "The happiness exercises include the body," Rachel says. "Cardio is not a reward after the metrics." Nancy pauses over the pen. "Leave it in. If it helps the work, it belongs before the work."
examples.whatToDo: Nancy yields without being overruled. She keeps 15 minutes of cardio in the plan and counts it as one of the happiness exercises, not as a treat after results.
examples.whyItMatters: The yield shows the order in action. Equal readers can disagree, then change course when the body practice supports the work they care about.

examples.title: The Stuck Zipper
examples.scenario: The locker zipper catches halfway while trainer Bryce stands by the bench, and the snag feels like permission to skip. Cardio is for people with clear afternoons. No, the list said 15 minutes, not a heroic workout. Happiness exercises are supposed to be small enough to repeat. The shoes are right there. He can still move before the mood votes no.
examples.whatToDo: Bryce lowers the bar back to the listed practice. He treats 15 minutes of cardio as the rep, not as a test of whether the whole day feels strong.
examples.whyItMatters: The wrong turn is familiar: friction gets read as a verdict. The practice asks for a small bodily rep before the mood turns one snag into a story.

examples.title: Porch Step Budget
examples.scenario: The cold glass sweats against Janet's palm while the back porch step cools under her heels. Her evening has room for one small plan, not a life reset. Shawn Achor's The Happiness Advantage has her circling happiness before success, so she budgets the next day on paper: 3 new things, one thank-you email, or 15 minutes of cardio.
examples.whatToDo: Janet allocates attention before the day begins. She uses Shawn Achor's happiness before success frame to pick one small rep that can survive a crowded schedule.
examples.whyItMatters: Planning first protects the practice from leftover time. Happiness becomes part of the slight-edge system before success gets to spend the whole day.

She waits to praise someone until her own mood improves.

questions.prompt: In the gym locker room, Yann treats mood work as purely mental and skips the gym bag. Which response fits the source list?

Mood work can include thanks, but body practice stays outside.
Mood work can include 15 minutes of cardio as practice.

choices: The list narrows daily practice to gratitude because it has a count.
The list offers savoring, forgiveness, giving, and reading 10 pages daily.
The list names cardio as the routine that replaces the others.
questions.explanation: The review names several practices, including savoring, forgiveness, giving, and reading 10 pages daily. It does not reduce happiness to one habit.

reviewCards.front: How does happiness before success change the order of work and mood?
reviewCards.back: It asks you to practice a better state before the win arrives. The review says happiness can support productivity, confidence, and motivation, so the mood is treated as fuel for action.

reviewCards.front: Why does writing 3 new things you are grateful for beat a vague positive attitude?
reviewCards.back: The count makes gratitude visible. You can check whether you wrote 3 new things, but you cannot check whether you were generally positive in any useful way.

reviewCards.front: Where does the body enter the happiness practices?

reviewCards.front: Recall seven-principle practice (Ch 13): name one concrete moment here where it actually bites.
reviewCards.back: Nancy keeps 15 minutes of cardio in the plan before the training day starts. That moment turns a principle into practice because she pays the price before results prove it was worth it.

reviewCards.back: They are gratitude, positive journaling, meditation, praise, cardio, savoring, forgiveness, giving, and reading. The list gives options, not one magic habit.

reviewCards.front: When does practicing happiness go wrong?
reviewCards.back: It goes wrong when the practice becomes a mask. Gratitude, cardio, or praise should support truthful action, not force a bright face over grief, stress, or a hard talk.

implementationPlan.title: Mark the Happiness Rep
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice happiness before success as one small marked rep. Pick one source-backed practice, such as 3 new things, a thanks email, or 15 minutes of cardio. Put a check beside the rep so the behavior is visible before the mood changes.

ifThenPlans.context: If the day starts with a win-first mood bargain,
ifThenPlans.plan: If you catch yourself waiting to feel okay until after success, then Mark the Happiness Rep. Write 3 new things you are grateful for and check the lines.

ifThenPlans.context: If your mood practice has become private and stale,
ifThenPlans.plan: If the next rep needs another person, then Mark the Happiness Rep with praise. Send one email thanking someone for a specific act.

ifThenPlans.context: If stress makes happiness feel like a thought problem only,
ifThenPlans.plan: If your body has been left out, then Mark the Happiness Rep with 15 minutes of cardio. Count the rep as practice, not as a workout test.

ifThenPlans.context: If the rep starts hiding grief or a hard conversation,
ifThenPlans.plan: If happiness practice turns into a mask, then pause Mark the Happiness Rep. Tell the truth first, then choose a rep that supports it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, the first time you touch the place where you set your keys, Mark the Happiness Rep: choose one practice, do it, and check it once.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Ask one other person to flag when you postpone feeling okay until after a win this week. Compare notes once, then pick one Happiness Rep you both saw you could mark earlier.

chapters.title: The Ripple Effect
chapters.hook: You hover over Send, and one small sentence is about to become the room's weather.
chapters.counterintuition: You may think the ripple effect is a nice closing image. In fact, it is social compounding: repeated choices become the environment someone else has to live in.
chapters.tryThisNow: At your next outgoing message today, pause in the reply window before Send. Cut one complaint line, rehearse a cleaner sentence once, then use only that.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Your small repeats do not stop at your skin; they shape the rooms, threads, mentors, and close associates that carry success or drift to someone else.

breakdown.fastRead: Your thumb is over Send, and the draft looks harmless: one jab about the late project, one joke about being broke, one shrug about skipping the helpful thing again. The myth says it is private. It is just your mood, your thread, your day. The ripple effect says the small act becomes part of somebody else's surroundings. Social compounding means repeated choices spread through people. Your discipline becomes someone else's weather. Before you send, ask what this line trains in the room you share.
breakdown.deepRead:
Hazel's arts chat changes before anyone calls it a habit. One person stops feeding the late-night complaint loop. Another brings an invoice question before rehearsal. A third notices that the cleaner tone is easier to copy than the old drift.

Tung M. Phung's review gives the plain social version: happiness and success depend partly on environment. Relationships, financial health, attitudes, success, and similar areas tend toward the average of the five closest associates. Use that as an audit, not a law with a calculator. Who gets first pull on your attention? Who makes a small healthy act feel normal? Who makes drift sound smart?

Presley and Hazel show the gentler side of the same force. A mentor and mentee do not form a one-way pipe. Hazel brings a blocked question, and Presley hears which studio habits still make sense to someone newer. The mutual benefit is the ripple. The older person gives a map; the newer person changes the map. A ripple can carry drift. It can also carry a standard.
breakdown.fullRead:
A closed door stops the ripple. If nobody sees the habit, hears the tone, or shares the channel, the effect stays private. That sounds obvious, but it saves you from overclaiming. A morning walk can help your body before it helps a friend. A quiet savings habit can steady you before it steadies a household. Social compounding starts when a choice becomes visible enough for another person to copy, answer, resist, or relax around.

Amazon's 8th Anniversary Edition placement gives the ripple a job, not a slogan. After the private disciplines, the last question is what those disciplines do to the air around you. A reader can admire the phrase and still send the sour reply, skip the useful call, or leave the younger worker guessing. The phrase only starts working when one small act changes the next person's options.

The five-associates idea is useful for the same reason. It is not a magic average, and it should not make you score friends like a spreadsheet. It asks a plain audit question: who makes the good action easier before you need willpower? If the same thread makes debt jokes sound normal, your financial health is already getting social input. If the same friend answers a tense message with patience, your relationships get a better cue.

One source transcript gives a simple warning: the Slight Edge can ripple for better or worse. That is why negative company needs care, not panic. The review does not ask you to cut off every hard person. It points to limits. Asher can stop the late-night debt-joke thread without ending lunch with the friend who sent it. You can reduce the pull of a sour channel and still keep a human tie intact.

The arts world gives the idea another surface. A Fractured Atlas application frames the source as useful for art, business, and life, and as a why-to more than a how-to. In plain terms, the reason behind the habit travels with the habit. If an artist only copies a tactic, the group gets a trick. If the group sees why invoices, rehearsal notes, or follow-up replies are part of the work, the standard can move through the whole arts ecosystem.

Mentor and mentee roles make the same point without a crowd. You seek a mentor because the upward curve is easier near someone who has walked longer. You take a mentee because your own standard gets clearer when someone else has to use it. Help is not only received; it is passed along while it is still warm.

The precondition is contact. A ripple needs a shared edge: a thread, a room, a habit in view, a question asked before the next person repeats the old pattern. Influence needs contact before it can travel. Without contact, the discipline may still matter deeply, but it will not yet become another person's environment.

examples.title: Stool Beside the Easel
examples.scenario: Mentor Presley slides the rehearsal stool toward Hazel before the Saturday arts co-op opens. "Mentor means I tell you what to do?" Hazel asks. "Mentee means you show me what I miss," Presley says. They are setting up a mutual benefit check-in: Hazel will bring one blocked grant question each week, and Presley will bring one studio habit she wants tested by someone newer.
examples.whatToDo: Presley makes the mentor meeting two-way before advice starts. She asks Hazel for one live problem and offers one habit for Hazel to question.
examples.whyItMatters: The mentor and mentee link becomes a ripple only when both people change. Advice lands better when the older person also has something to learn.

examples.title: Couch Ping Audit
examples.scenario: Chantal is sorting her five closest associates on the living-room couch when the bank app pings and an unanswered voice memo drops below it. She expects the problem to be money, because the rent transfer is short. The reveal is smaller and worse: the broke-joke thread has been shaping her attitudes before she checks her financial health. One ghosted reply has also cooled a relationship she meant to keep.
examples.whatToDo: Chantal answers the voice memo first, then moves the broke-joke thread out of the first slot she sees when money feels tight.
examples.whyItMatters: The five closest associates idea is not income trivia. It asks which relationships and attitudes get to steer financial health before a choice is made.

examples.title: Lunch Break Thread
examples.scenario:
There is not much lunch break left, and prep cook Tobias keeps the group chat open in the alley while the shift lead waits for his answer.
Asher: Are you in for the rant thread tonight?
Tobias: I am limiting that one this week.
Asher: Cutting us off?
Tobias: No. Five closest associates, relationships, financial health. Stiff phrase, useful check.
Asher: So lunch tomorrow?
Tobias: Lunch stays.
examples.whatToDo: Tobias limits the negative thread for the week and keeps the direct lunch plan. He changes exposure without making the relationship disposable.
examples.whyItMatters: Positive and like-minded people matter, but the source does not require social exile. The small boundary protects attention while leaving a tie alive.

examples.title: Rehearsal Notes Reset
examples.scenario: The rehearsal notes are good, and the replies underneath them are sour. Stage manager Hazel is about to add one more sharp line in the arts workers' chat when she stops, closes the draft, and restarts. Her five closest associates have been shaping her attitudes and relationships all week; the financial health joke is already turning into a plan. She writes one clean ask instead: who can review invoices before the meeting?
examples.whatToDo: Hazel stops the complaint draft and restarts with a practical request. She uses the same channel to make a better next action easier to copy.
examples.whyItMatters: A reset is small enough to miss. That is why it works here: the social cue changes before the group has to recover from a colder tone.

examples.title: Pickup Line Lesson
examples.scenario: "The mentor gets more out of this than the mentee," someone says in the school pickup line, and volunteer coordinator Cyrus stops folding the permission slip. Across the asphalt, a student teacher balances poster board against one hip while an older teacher marks tomorrow's names on tape. The mutual benefit is quiet: one gets a map for the first year, and the other hears which examples still make sense to a new person.
examples.whatToDo: Cyrus copies the pairing into the volunteer roster: each mentor brings one tested routine, and each mentee brings one question from the new-person view.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene keeps mentoring from becoming status theater. A useful ripple moves both directions, from experience to practice and back again.

examples.title: Teller Window Revision
examples.scenario: "Just ignore them for a month," freelance designer Asher says at the bank teller window, deposit slip in hand. The glass throws his own face back at him. He is rehearsing a reply about a friend's debt joke, but the words sound cruel. The five closest associates idea includes relationships and financial health; it does not turn people into trash. Asher scratches out ignore, writes limit the late-night thread, and leaves the lunch invite alone.
examples.whatToDo: Asher corrects the harsh draft before sending it. He limits the negative channel and protects the relationship that still deserves care.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery keeps the association audit humane. The useful move is managed exposure, not pretending a difficult person has no value.

questions.prompt: A bookseller labels the Ripple Effect as a stray add-on, separate from the anniversary material. Which correction fits the source record?
choices: It belongs with the early philosophy setup, before the later edition material begins.
It belongs with the 8th Anniversary Edition material, not a stray add-on.
It belongs with a later finance appendix, outside the anniversary framing.
questions.explanation: The product record ties the Ripple Effect to the 8th Anniversary Edition. The add-on reading misses that it is part of the edition's closing extension.

questions.prompt: A wellness group says happiness is only a private mindset, so the room and companions do not matter. What is the best reply?
choices: Happiness should be judged mainly by private effort, with surroundings treated as background noise.
Happiness also depends on the environment around the person, not just inner effort.
Happiness should be measured through income first, with mood handled after money improves.
questions.explanation: The source adds environment to the happiness picture. Private effort still matters, but surroundings are part of the ripple mechanism.

questions.prompt: A coach teaches the five-associates idea as income math only. What is missing from that reading?
choices: The review applies the average mainly to public reputation, with money treated as a side effect.
The review applies the average only to spending habits, with relationships outside the pattern.
The review applies the average to relationships, financial health, attitudes, success, and related areas.
questions.explanation: The closest-five idea is wider than income. The review names relationships, financial health, attitudes, success, and related areas.

questions.prompt: A student says association is fixed; the people around him are just the people around him. Which next move matches the review?
choices: He should observe the group for a while without changing who gets most of his time.
He should wait for the group to change before he changes his own daily routines.
He should spend more chosen time near positive, like-minded companions.
questions.explanation: The review treats social input as something a person can shape. Choosing positive, like-minded people is the advised move.

questions.prompt: A reader drafts a message after a cousin drains another call with complaint. "If someone is negative, the slight-edge answer is to delete them from my life," she writes. What nuance is missing?
choices: The review points to keeping difficult contact unchanged so the tie feels safer for now.
The review points to replacing hard conversations with silent distance and no stated edge.
The review points to limiting exposure, especially when rejection would harm close ties.
questions.explanation: The source gives a middle path. Limiting time with negative people protects the environment without making cutoff the default answer.

questions.prompt: A designer seeks a mentor but refuses to help the newer intern because she has nothing to spare. What does the ripple idea add?
choices: She should seek senior advice until her own work feels secure enough to share.
She should value mentor and mentee roles because influence can move both ways.
She should teach after her mentor has already solved the next step for her.
questions.explanation: The review names both mentor and mentee relationships. The ripple is reciprocal: receiving help and giving help can both shape success.

questions.prompt: An arts worker says the principle belongs in personal finance, not in the studio budget or rehearsal room. Which correction fits the application?
choices: It can carry into art, business, and life, not only money choices.
It should stay inside private goals until the arts work has settled.
It belongs mainly to sales tactics once creative work is set aside.
questions.explanation: The arts application broadens the field. It frames the principle as useful for art, business, and life, not just personal finance.

questions.prompt: During a volunteer project kickoff, the lead says, "Just give the group the tactic; motivation is extra." What does this miss?
choices: The application frames the idea as a why-to, so meaning helps the tactic travel.
The application frames the idea as a checklist, so meaning can wait until later.
The application frames the idea as a finance tip, so group purpose sits beside the task.
questions.explanation: The source calls the material a why-to, not only a how-to. In a community, the reason behind the habit helps others copy it.

questions.prompt: A team leader assumes small habits can only spread good effects through the group. What should she plan for?
choices: Small habits can ripple for better or worse, so drift needs the same attention as progress.
Small habits spread after results are visible, so drift can be reviewed at the finish.
Small habits stay private until a leader names them, so group effects are rare.
questions.explanation: The ripple can run in either direction. Planning only for the positive side ignores how small negative patterns can also spread.

reviewCards.front: What does social compounding mean in plain words?
reviewCards.back: It means repeated choices do not stay private. They shape the people, rooms, threads, and standards around you, and those surroundings then influence other people.

reviewCards.front: Why is the five-associates idea an audit, not a reason to cut people off?
reviewCards.back: It asks who is shaping relationships, financial health, attitudes, and success. The useful response may be more chosen exposure or less exposure, not automatic rejection.

reviewCards.front: How do mentor and mentee roles create a ripple in both directions?
reviewCards.back: The mentor passes on a tested path, while the mentee shows what still works for someone newer. Both people adjust, so the relationship becomes input and contribution.

reviewCards.front: Why must a ripple plan watch drift as closely as progress?
reviewCards.back: The ripple can spread for better or worse. A small complaint, skipped standard, or careless joke can travel through a group just as a useful habit can.

reviewCards.front: Which matters more here, boredom as evidence of repeatability (Ch 8) or social compounding, and why?
reviewCards.back: Ch 8 helps you keep a dull useful act. Here the sharper issue is where that act travels: a small repeat can change the people, channels, and rooms around you.

reviewCards.front: What precondition does the ripple effect quietly assume?
reviewCards.back: It assumes contact. A choice has to be visible, shared, or felt in an environment before it can become part of another person's surroundings.

implementationPlan.title: Run the Ripple Pause
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice pausing before a small act becomes someone else's input. Run the Ripple Pause means you ask, before a reply, meeting note, or request: what will this train in the next person? Then stop one behavior that spreads drift and send the cleaner signal.

ifThenPlans.context: If a reply starts with a complaint that others could copy
ifThenPlans.plan: If the draft spreads drift, then Run the Ripple Pause: cut the complaint line and write one request someone can act on.

ifThenPlans.context: If a group chat pulls you toward the same negative loop
ifThenPlans.plan: If the thread keeps lowering your standard, then Run the Ripple Pause: limit that channel for the day and choose one positive contact.

ifThenPlans.context: If asking for a mentor starts to feel one-way
ifThenPlans.plan: If guidance feels like taking, then Run the Ripple Pause: bring one useful question and one way your newer view can help the mentor.

ifThenPlans.context: If a creative meeting treats habits as private extras
ifThenPlans.plan: If the group wants only tactics, then Run the Ripple Pause: name the reason for the habit and the one standard the room can copy.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, stage one reply before sending it. Open the draft, remove one line that spreads drift, and rehearse one cleaner sentence in the message window.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, move one negative thread lower in your message list and pin one positive or mentor channel above it. Notice which standard gets first pull.

memorableLines.why: It makes the social cost of a private habit easy to feel.

memorableLines.text: A ripple can carry drift.
memorableLines.why: It keeps the reader from hearing ripple as only good news.

memorableLines.text: Influence needs contact before it can travel.
